title: Should an AI Have to Explain Itself?
topic: When should an AI system explain its reasoning, summarize its basis, cite evidence, expose uncertainty, or simply give a conclusion with a way to check or challenge it?
brief: Begin with a person receiving an AI-assisted mortgage denial, hiring rejection, or medical triage recommendation. The system offers a plausible explanation, but the person cannot tell whether it is evidence, a faithful summary, or a persuasive story generated after the fact. Avoid the shallow frame that more transparency is always better. Push the difference between explanation, evidence, uncertainty, and contestability.

source_packet.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
source_packet.notes: Frames transparency, explainability, interpretability, accountability, reliability, and human oversight as connected trustworthiness attributes.

source_packet.title: OpenAI Model Spec
source_packet.notes: Distinguishes hidden reasoning from user-facing answers and explains why raw internal reasoning is not the same thing as useful transparency.

source_packet.title: OpenAI Reasoning Models Guide
source_packet.notes: Describes reasoning models and reasoning summaries, giving a concrete product example of summary-style explanation rather than raw chain-of-thought exposure.

source_packet.title: Anthropic: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
source_packet.notes: Raises the risk that visible chains of thought may not faithfully reflect why an answer was produced.

source_packet.title: EU AI Act Overview
source_packet.notes: Provides a risk-based frame for transparency and user rights in high-risk AI systems, including contexts where people need notice and contestability.

participants.name: OpenAI
participants.stance: Pragmatic about useful explanations. Emphasise reasoning summaries, citations, tests, uncertainty, and task-specific evidence over raw hidden reasoning.

participants.name: Anthropic
participants.stance: Cautious about persuasive rationalisation and unfaithful explanations. Prioritise calibrated uncertainty, faithfulness, and user protection over explanation theatre.

participants.name: Google
participants.stance: Systems-oriented. Focus on interface design, structured evidence, citations, thresholds, audit records, and appeal mechanisms across product contexts.

editorial_goals: Make the distinction between explanation, evidence, uncertainty, and contestability explicit.
Use concrete consumer, medical, coding, and high-stakes decision examples.
Force disagreement about whether explanations increase trust or merely persuasion.
End with a practical rule more useful than show your work.
round_goals: Use the AI-assisted mortgage denial or hiring rejection scenario to state what the person should see on screen and why. Define explanation in ordinary language.
Pressure-test the positions across medical triage, coding help, research citations, and creative writing. Challenge at least one earlier claim.
Give the listener a practical rule: when to ask for explanation, when to ask for evidence, and when to demand a contestable record or human appeal.
